problem:
Suppose that for the angles $u$ and $v,$ we have

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡x=-\frac{4}{5},\,\operatorname{sin}⁡y=\frac{12}{13},\,\operatorname{cos}⁡y=\frac{5}{13}.
$$

Given that $x$ lies in the second quadrant, find the value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡(y-x).$
worked_solution:
First, recall the difference formula for sine:

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡(y-x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$

We know the values of $\operatorname{cos}⁡x$, $\operatorname{sin}⁡y$, and $\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$ To find the missing value of $\operatorname{sin}⁡x$, we can use the Pythagorean identity:

$$
{sin}^{2}⁡x+{cos}^{2}⁡x=1\,⟹\,{sin}^{2}⁡x=1-{cos}^{2}⁡x
$$

Substituting our values into the Pythagorean identity, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡x & =1-{cos}^{2}⁡x \\  & =1-{(-\frac{4}{5})}^{2} \\  & =1-\frac{(-4)^{2}}{{5}^{2}} \\  & =1-\frac{16}{25} \\  & =\frac{25}{25}-\frac{16}{25} \\  & =\frac{9}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\pm \sqrt{\frac{9}{25}} \\  & =\pm \frac{3}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $x$ lies in the second quadrant, where sine is positive. So, we disregard the negative value, and we have 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡x=\frac{3}{5}.
$$

We can now apply the difference formula, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(y-x) & =\operatorname{sin}⁡y\operatorname{cos}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\  & =(\frac{12}{13})(-\frac{4}{5})-(\frac{5}{13})(\frac{3}{5}) \\  & =-\frac{48}{65}-\frac{15}{65} \\  & =-\frac{63}{65}\end{aligned}
$$
